opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been one of the most important parts of how we work. The way I think about it, our team spends a lot of time figuring out what the product should actually do. What are the tasks people really care about? What does a great output look like? Where are the models falling short today? The RL team has the infrastructure and expertise to turn that into training improvements.

So a big part of the collaboration is translating product intuition into something trainable. That means building datasets and environments that reflect real use cases, and defining what good looks like in a way you can actually grade. If you want a model that's great at browsing and synthesizing information, you need tasks hard enough to require real multi-step reasoning, plus a reliable way to tell whether the model got it right. Much of the work goes into designing those tasks and graders carefully, because the model will optimize for whatever you reward, including the shortcuts you didn't intend.

What's exciting is how tight the feedback loop has become. We'll see a failure in testing, like the model giving up too early on a search, not checking its sources, or being overconfident, and we can go back, build data that targets that behavior, and see it improve in the next round. That's very different from the older approach, where you mostly hoped capabilities would emerge from pretraining and then patched things with prompting.

I also think it works well because the line between research and product is pretty blurry for us. People on our team understand the training side, and the RL researchers care a lot about how the product feels to use. That shared context lets you move quickly. You're not throwing requirements over a wall. You're iterating together on the model and the experience at the same time.

Longer term, I think this is how many agentic capabilities will get unlocked. You pick a domain where you can define tasks and measure success, invest heavily in high-quality environments and evaluation, and let RL push the model further than you'd get otherwise. The hard part, and the fun part, is picking the right problems and defining success well.

r001.rationale: The response says the RL team turns product needs into training improvements and describes joint iteration, but it does not explain that those improvements compound by giving Isa Fulford’s team a stronger base model to train further.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the collaboration is really the whole story, honestly. The way I'd describe it is that on the post-training and product side, we're very close to what people actually want the model to do. We see the tasks, we see where it falls over, we see the weird edge cases that only show up when real users are hammering on something. And the RL team is building the machinery that lets the model actually get better at those things through practice rather than just through imitation.

So the loop looks something like: we go and figure out what a really good task looks like. Not just "answer this question," but something with a real environment, real tools, a real notion of success. For something like deep research, that's "can you go browse, find the right sources, synthesize them, and come back with something a person would actually trust." And then we work with the RL team to turn that into something the model can be trained against, where it tries, gets feedback, and improves.

What's been striking to me is how much the task design matters. The algorithms are obviously a huge part of it, but if you give the model a bad environment or a reward that's easy to game, it will find the shortcut every time. So a lot of our contribution is being the people who understand the domain well enough to say, "no, that's not actually what good looks like," and iterating on that with them.

And the other thing I'd say is that it's very bidirectional. We'll bring a capability we want, and they'll tell us what's realistic or what the training signal needs to look like. Or they'll have a new method that unlocks something, and we'll go find the use case where it really shines. The teams that are set up as a tight loop like that, rather than a handoff, are the ones that end up shipping things that feel like a step change.

r001.rationale: The response describes collaboration on task design, feedback, and RL training, but does not say that RL improvements compound by giving Isa Fulford’s team a stronger base model to train further.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really useful feedback loop. When you’re building products with these models, you see where they’re capable and where they still struggle—especially on tasks that involve multiple steps or using tools. We can bring those concrete examples to the reinforcement learning team and work together on what better behavior would look like and how to measure it.

Then, as the models improve, that opens up new things we can build, which exposes the next set of limitations. So the collaboration helps connect improvements in model capabilities to whether the model can actually accomplish something useful for a user.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a really useful feedback loop. Our team sees how people are actually using the models, where they’re getting stuck, and what kinds of tasks they want to accomplish. We can bring those concrete examples to the reinforcement learning team and work together on what better behavior should look like and how to measure it.

Then, as the models improve, we can put them into real workflows and see whether those improvements translate into something useful. A model might do better on an evaluation, but the question is whether it can help someone complete a task more reliably. That collaboration helps us connect the research to what users need.
